findings.title: Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are dropped after the first rebalance
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and the same instance is handed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy at each partition revoke. `close()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown=True`, shuts every queue and joins the workers. The next `create_with_partitions` reuses the dead pool. Its workers have exited and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception, logs it, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`. Every message after the first rebalance is therefore silently dropped and its offset is committed, which is data loss. The shared `OffsetTracker` also keeps stale `last_committed` and `all_offsets` state across assignments. The strategy should not own or shut down the pool (the factory's `shutdown()` should), or the pool must be created per strategy.

findings.title: Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread
findings.body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`. In the factory that wraps arroyo's `commit` callback, which stages offsets on the `KafkaConsumer` and may commit. That state is owned by the `StreamProcessor` thread and is not designed for concurrent access while the main thread is polling, pausing or rebalancing. The loop can also commit offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which raises inside the thread; the exception is swallowed and retried every second. Commits should be driven from `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread, using the tracker's committable offsets, rather than from a separate thread.

findings.title: Unbounded queues and no MessageRejected, despite the documented 'natural backpressure'
findings.body: The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises arroyo's `MessageRejected`. If one worker stalls on a slow item, the consumer keeps polling and enqueueing. Memory grows without bound and the backlog is never limited by the poll loop. The offset tracker's `all_offsets` and `outstanding` sets also grow because the stuck offset blocks all later commits. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

findings.title: Gap detection only works until the first commit; later gaps are skipped
findings.body: `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` skips any gap between `last_committed` and the smallest tracked offset. `mark_committed` prunes `all_offsets` to offsets above the committed one. With offsets 100, 102, 103 tracked, the first pass commits 100. The next pass sees `all_offsets={102,103}`, `start=102`, and commits 103 without 101 ever being tracked or completed. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (and the uptime gaps test) do not catch this: the first one passes because it submits 101 before the second commit can matter, and the other only checks the first commit. The documented guarantee ('only commits when all prior offsets are processed') is not enforced. Contiguity should be checked against `last_committed + 1`, or the tracker should rely on in-order submission explicitly.

findings.title: Docstring claims offsets are committed only after successful processing
findings.body: The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised. Failed items therefore become committable and are committed, so processing errors are skipped rather than retried. The docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is wrong. Similarly, `terminate()` calls `shutdown()` with `immediate=False`, which does not actually terminate quickly.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only by timing
findings.body: The docstring says 'errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the test asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. With the actual implementation both offsets (the failing one included) are completed in the worker's `finally` and would be committed by the commit loop after its 1s wait. The assertion passes only because the test checks within about 0.3s, before the first commit tick. It verifies nothing about error handling and will fail or flake if timing changes. It should wait for a commit and assert that offsets 100 and 101 are committed (as 102), or assert the intended behavior explicitly.

findings.title: Flaky assertions on queue depth and on hash distribution
findings.body: `test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0` right after submitting 10 items to live worker threads. The workers only append to a list, so they can drain everything before the check. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python string hashes are randomized per process, so this fails for a small fraction of runs (about 0.1%). Both should avoid depending on timing or on the hash seed, for example by blocking the processor on an event or by choosing keys with known assignments.
